video.title: He Spends 1 Hour a Week on This Business

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jay Meldrum, who left corporate professional services to open Swing Cave Golf, a single-bay members-only golf simulator in a Texas strip mall (Allen area). Six months in he has about 28 members on three tiers (USD 175/275/325 per month), roughly USD 7,000 monthly revenue, break-even at about 15 members after three months, and claimed 50-55% net margins. The business is run with 24/7 app-based door access, scheduling software and cameras, with about an hour a week of owner time. Upfront cost is about USD 100K, and he plans a second location and eventual scaling. Takeaway: a low-opex, membership-based, physical-space business can be near-passive once built, but it needs significant capital and a physical site.

speakers.name: Jay Meldrum
speakers.description: Founder of Swing Cave Golf, ex-corporate professional services, retired early

ideas.name: Swing Cave Golf - private membership golf simulator bay
ideas.one_liner: Single-bay indoor golf simulator in a retail unit rented on monthly memberships with 24/7 app door access.
ideas.business_model: Monthly membership tiers plus punch cards; members book tee times for private use of the bay
ideas.customer: Golf enthusiasts who want to practise privately: country club members, beginners intimidated by ranges, families wanting a private space; neighbourhood residents within a few miles
ideas.problem: Golfers want a place to practise in bad weather or privately, and home simulators take up space and sit unused about 23 hours a day
ideas.offer: Private single-bay simulator with accurate swing data and games, 24/7 access, up to 2-hour tee times, unlimited guests per session

pricing.model: Tiered monthly membership plus punch cards
pricing.notes: Priced at market, not undercutting. Punch cards of 5 and 10 added later, valid 6 months, up to 1 hour per session. Members get up to 2 hours per session. Transcript is ambiguous on tier session counts (said 40/80 then 4/8).

acquisition_channels.details: Pre-sold to about 5 committed friends before opening, who gave feedback; about 15 of 28 members are people he knew from church, work, sports and neighbourhood; no grand opening or marketing yet

quote.text: We haven't really done a lot of marketing.
quote.speaker: Jay Meldrum

acquisition_channels.details: Passing road frontage visibility; neighbours walked in after seeing the unit; the other 13-14 members came from friends or seeing the unit while driving past

ideas.delivery: Customers self-serve: they get an email with tee time, and 10 minutes before the phone app unlocks the door. Owner spends about an hour a week cleaning and taking out trash with his son, and watches via cameras. Scheduling runs on a software platform.
unit_economics_claims: About USD 7,000 monthly revenue at 28 members
Break-even around 15 members, reached in about 3 months
Max capacity about 40 members per bay, about USD 100K revenue per year claimed
Rent about USD 31 per sq ft
tools: Simulator software subscription (about USD 100 per year)
ideas.startup_cost: About USD 100K upfront for equipment and fit-out; lease clause meant no rent until opening; landlord improvement allowance negotiated
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Opened September; pre-opening friends committed; break-even in about 3 months

acquisition.how: Currently word of mouth and location visibility; could add SEO, Google Business Profile and paid local ads, but still depends on a physical site and neighbours

onboarding.how: Online sign-up and automated access; occasional manual walkthrough via camera ping for new members

delivery.how: Door access and booking are automated, but the physical space needs cleaning, trash removal and equipment upkeep by a human

billing.how: Recurring membership billing through the software platform

support.how: Cameras and remote ping; chatbot or agent could handle FAQs, but equipment faults and issues need an on-site human

uk_applicability.notes: Model works in the UK, but needs commercial lease, planning/change-of-use, insurance, higher rent and cold-weather demand in the UK is arguably strong. A 100K-equivalent capital outlay is large for a part-time solo founder; UK golf simulator demand exists but pricing in GBP would differ.

risks: High upfront capital of about USD 100K
Capacity cap of about 40 members per bay
Churn if members stop using it
Margin claims are unaudited and based on early months

tactics.name: Pre-sell to friends before opening
steps: Talk to 10+ friends and acquaintances before opening
Get verbal commitments from about 5 who are all in
Use the first early member for product feedback
Use feedback to adjust amenities (e.g., club straps, storage)

quote.text: I just need these 10 friends and my costs are at least covered and I'm breaking even.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Tiered membership with caps
steps: Offer three tiers by visit count (Par/Birdie/Eagle) at 175/275/325
Add punch cards (5 and 10, 6-month expiry) for occasional users
Target a mix of enthusiasts rather than daily users
Cap members at about 35-40 per bay to keep tee times available

tactics.name: Take over a failing tenant's lease
steps: Find a unit whose tenant is in trouble
Offer the landlord to step into the lease at 15% off the current rent
Use a real estate attorney friend to get tenant improvement allowance

quote.text: If you give me 15% off of their current rent, I will step into their lease
quote.speaker: Jay Meldrum

tactics.name: Location choice near homes
steps: Pick a unit within about 5 miles of the owner's home
Prefer neighbourhood proximity and road frontage over shopping-centre footfall
Check roughly 100,000 people within 5 miles for 40 members

tactics.name: Low-touch operations via automation
steps: Use scheduling software to book tee times
Email confirmation then phone app unlocks the door 10 minutes before
Use cameras to monitor and ping new members for walkthrough
Owner or family cleans about one hour a week

warnings.warning: Customers who use it every day reduce capacity, while customers who rarely use it risk churn; aim for enthusiasts but not obsessives
Other businesses in the same strip mall had not done well, so location risk is real

quote.text: there have been other businesses in this strip mall that haven't done well.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Build for a customer of one: designing the business around your own need makes decisions and persistence easier.

quote.text: I think anything entrepreneurial if you're passionate about it, it's a lot easier to do.
quote.speaker: Jay Meldrum

lessons.lesson: Pre-sell to a small group of friends to validate demand and reduce break-even risk before spending on fit-out.
Negotiate lease terms (no rent until opening, improvement allowances) to cut risk on physical businesses.
Membership models with capped capacity give predictable recurring revenue and a break-even benchmark (15 of 40 members).
Passive income is rarely passive; the effort is front-loaded, and this one still needs a physical footprint and capital.

quote.text: nothing is passive. Yeah. Because if something is passive, you have to do a lot of active work to get to that point.
quote.speaker: Jay Meldrum

lessons.lesson: Don't wait for perfect conditions; learning from early members before permits arrived was valuable.

quote.text: if you really want to do it, just do it. You learn more by doing it than thinking about it.
quote.speaker: Jay Meldrum

lessons.lesson: Price at market and compete on product quality rather than undercutting.
Use the second location to test the opposite strategy (heavy marketing) versus the first (word of mouth only).

evidence_quality.rationale: First-hand operator with specific numbers (members, tiers, costs) that are mostly consistent, but only six months of data, margin claims are unverified and partly projected, and the transcript is Whisper-tiny with some garbled numbers.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Host sells a USD 19 golf simulator business plan and sponsors Bizee.
